title: corerules Content Pack, format version 0.1
description: Canonical schema, authored by the corpus-v1 map (ticket 05 spine, ticket 14 shapes). Covers the ten kinds the proving slice needs, not all 27. Enforcement is two-tiered: what is declared here, and what the validator checks. Recursive structures, numeric ranges and cross-field rules are the validator's. **Correction 55 — the canonical serialisation.** A pack file is `json.dumps(obj, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)` followed by one newline, with keys in the order they were written. This cannot be a schema rule — a JSON Schema sees a parsed document and never its bytes — so `tools/validate.py` reports it and `tools/normalise.py` fixes it. It is here because §7.1 chose a directory of JSON FOR diffability, and a format with no canonical form serves that only by luck: twice in two sessions a script that changed five effects reserialised 24,708 lines, because five of the pack's 27 files were written with one space of indentation and the other 22 with two.

id.description: Pack-scoped, opaque, derived from the source anchor (ticket 07). '#n' discriminates records sharing one source file.

provenance.description: Ticket 05: replaces §7.1's book-and-page, which this corpus cannot supply. 'section' is for a human holding the printed book; 'anchor' is for the machine, and is what the id derives from. **Correction 6:** `anchor` is no longer unconditionally required. §5.1 says the house-rule escape hatch IS the pack, and a hand-authored record has no rendition and no source file to point into — so requiring one forbade the very pack §5.1 promised. What the record must carry follows from the manifest's `provenanceMode`, and that condition spans two FILES, which a JSON Schema cannot see: the checker enforces it, counted apart from schema errors for the same reason duplicate ids are (correction 40). `section` stays required, because a record with no place at all is not provenance in either mode.

anchor.description: Where in the source bytes. REQUIRED when the manifest declares `provenanceMode: extracted` and FORBIDDEN when it declares `hand-authored` — an anchor claims a rendition of a source the pack has just said it does not have.

interpretation.description: Ticket 11: the book is ambiguous and this record is a reading. Absent means the source was unambiguous — never that nobody looked.

scalar.description: Ticket 06: the only scalars a predicate or operand may name. 'level' is ALWAYS qualified by class — the unqualified form does not exist, because §6.1's sum type means Fighter 5 / Mage 4 has no 'level 5'. WIDENED by ticket 13 finding 136. Two arms were too narrow by exactly the things a character most obviously IS: 206 conditions named `{ability: 'phb:race'}` and `{ability: 'phb:alignment'}` — race is not an ability and no record answers to those ids, so every one of them was a lie the schema accepted. The third arm is a FIELD PATH, which makes the format symmetric: effects WRITE field paths and predicates READ them, in one vocabulary rather than two. It also closes a second abuse with the same shape — `computedOperand.of` naming `phb:spell-duration` to say 'double the duration', where what it wants is the current value of the field being adjusted.

field.description: A field path, in the same vocabulary the effects write.

dice.description: Ticket 15 decision 1, implemented here by ticket 13 finding 42 — the decision was settled and the schema had no pattern at all. A §3.3 VALUE TYPE: no id, never referenced by `record`. Not yet referenced by any kind either, because the kinds that carry dice (generation methods, wealth options) are outside the proving slice. The decision states the grammar as 'NdM+-k'. Measured over the v1 RTF: 2,574 notations, of which 77.9% are NdM and 17.4% NdM+-k — and 4.7% (121) are NdM x k, which that grammar REJECTS. So the multiplier is admitted. A bare 'd10' with no count is admitted for the same reason: the corpus writes it. WIDENED by finding 79: the first pattern assumed the grammar 'NdM [xK] [±J]' in that order, and the corpus also writes '(NdM ± J) x K' — 14 occurrences including the wizard's standard starting money, '(1d4+1) x 10 gp'. Grouping changes the arithmetic, so this is not a notation variant but a different expression, and the first pattern silently rejected it.

operand.description: Ticket 15: known unknown #4 fired — 31 corpus occurrences of halving, division and rounding inside kit effects. NOT a seventh operation: 'adjust' still sums, only its operand widens. Used by effects AND by predicate values, since the arithmetic appears on both sides. WIDENED by ticket 13 finding 110: a fourth arm for `N on 1dM`, which is a value the corpus states directly and no arithmetic over integers can recover. WIDENED AGAIN by ticket 13 finding 118: a fifth arm for a PLAIN die. Finding 110 gave `dice` a consumer only as a threshold — `1-5 on 1d6` — and a hit die is the die itself as a value, which the four groups state in one sentence each: `set hitDice.perLevel to 1d10`.

computedOperand.description: Closed set, not general arithmetic. Rounding is a property of the operand — which is where §7.2's requirement finally lands.

condition.description: Ticket 06: a closed, flat vocabulary — compare, member, has. Race lists are membership and unless/except are §4.3's 'except'. Boolean combination lives one level up in 'clause', never here: a condition is a leaf, which is what keeps the evaluator a loop instead of a recursive descent.

clause.description: Ticket 13 finding 10, repairing ticket 06. Disjunction was measured at 4 occurrences by a regex that required '<Ab> N ... or ... <Ab>'; the corpus writes '<Ab> or <Ab> N', which occurs 38 times, and four v1 kits need it: the Homesteader and Bandit as 'A and (B or C)', the Goblinsticker and Smuggler as a bare 'A or B'. So a clause is a condition or a disjunction of conditions, and NOTHING ELSE: one level, no recursion, no 'or' of 'and'. Both corpus examples are that shape, and it keeps the evaluator flat, which is what ticket 06 was actually defending. Negation is still absent — finding 7's 33 occurrences remain text.

predicate.description: A flat list of clauses; every clause must hold. Ticket 13 finding 10 widened the entries from conditions to clauses, so a single entry may be a disjunction.

effect.description: §4.3's six operations as a discriminated union, so an operation carrying the wrong fields is UNREPRESENTABLE rather than merely invalid — §5's 'illegal states are unrepresentable', and §6.1's principle: structural for model incoherence, pack-declared for game rules. Ticket 13 finding 108: an effect may carry its own `provenance`. A record's effects are not necessarily all from one book — `phb:dwarf` is the PHB's record and 28 of its effects are the Complete Book of Dwarves re-scoring the PHB's proficiencies. Without this the pack asserts that the core rules say something they do not.

text.description: §4.3: anything outside the vocabulary is carried as text and not computed.

unmodelled.description:
**Correction 45.** True where `text` is a TRANSCRIBER'S MARKER — the effect was modelled as far as the format allowed and what was left over is written down. Present only when true; its absence means the text, if any, is ordinary commentary.

**A field because a string search is not a classifier.** The convention was typographic — `UNMODELLED <CATEGORY>:` — and it had already drifted: 286 markers, of which six are punctuated differently (`UNMODELLED CAP only:`, `UNMODELLED as a cap:`, `UNMODELLED CONDITIONS, as for the elf:`), and prose that merely MENTIONS the word reads as a marker to any regex. That false positive has now been introduced twice by people repairing the markers themselves, which is the argument in one sentence.

Engine ticket 02 decided the marker's declared CATEGORY stays prose and the Engine branches on the operation instead. This is not that: it says only WHETHER an effect is marked, which the Engine has to know to keep it out of a total.

optional.description:
**Correction 57.** True where the BOOK marks this rule optional — *'the DM may decide that the character … gets a +5% bonus … but if he has both, he gets a +10% bonus'*, *'only where the optional weapon specialization rules are in use'*. Present only when true.

**Correction 59: it names the option.** §3.4 makes rule-set names the Engine's closed catalogue — *'the Engine cannot act on a name it does not understand'* — and no catalogue existed anywhere until `spec.md` §5.5 was written. **This enum IS that catalogue**, transcribed from the 28 sections the Player's Handbook and the DMG head *'(Optional Rule)'* in their own words, cut to the eight inside v1's scope. It is the one place in the schema where an enumeration is closed on purpose — §3.4's single exception — and it grows by specification, never by a pack.

**It is a third thing and neither §5.1 nor §6.2 reaches it.** A3 has a pack declare which rule-sets it PROVIDES, which is about validation coverage; §5.2 puts computation rules in the Engine, *'never optional pack data'*. This is a rule inside a set the pack does provide, that a TABLE decides to use, and that changes a NUMBER. §5.1 claims A3 subsumes the optional DMG rule; for a computation it does not.

An optional effect is fully modelled — this is not `unmodelled`. What is unknown is not the rule but whether this table plays it, so §5.5 withholds it from the total and shows it with the option named, and a Character records the options its campaign uses.

provenance.description: Present only when this effect comes from a DIFFERENT book than the record does.
Present only when this effect comes from a DIFFERENT book than the record does.
Present only when this effect comes from a DIFFERENT book than the record does.

oneOf.description: §4.3: 'except' names the SUBJECT, not the prohibition — which is what keeps Effects from needing identity (§3.3).

provenance.description: Present only when this effect comes from a DIFFERENT book than the record does.
Present only when this effect comes from a DIFFERENT book than the record does.

record.description: What every pack kind carries. Value types (§3.3) deliberately do NOT reference this: they have no id, which is how §3's three-way split is enforced structurally.

alsoPrinted.description: **Correction 56.** The other names the books print for this thing. §7.3 says a name is never identity; this is the bill for that being true — **the corpus's naming is consistent WITHIN a table and not BETWEEN tables**, and four corrections each built a private map and threw it away. The Player's Handbook alone prints the two-handed sword as `Two-hand. sword` in Table 44 and `2-hd Sword` in Table 41, and the warhammer as `Warhammer` in Table 44 and `Hammer` in Table 45; the Complete Priest's permit-lists write `sword/long` where Table 44 writes `Long sword`.\n\nFor RESOLVING prose into ids, and nothing else. It is not a display name and the Engine never shows it: `name` is what a reader sees. An alias must resolve uniquely within its kind, which the checker enforces — `mace` is deliberately absent, because the Player's Handbook prints a footman's and a horseman's mace and the Complete Priest's says only 'mace'. **An ambiguity the books really have must not be hidden in a lookup table.**

attachable.description: §4.1: ONE closed shape used three times. Kit, Deity and Subrace each extend this and add only their target and cardinality — the two things §4.1 says they cannot share. Expressed structurally so that if the claim is wrong, it breaks here rather than after transcription.

effectsModelled.description: Ticket 13, found by running the extractor: without this, a mechanically extracted record with `effects: []` validates as a COMPLETE record with no effects. That is A3's own distinction — 'does not restrict' versus 'not transcribed yet' — missing one level down. §5.1 put it on the pack; a record needs it too, because extraction produces the incomplete state by construction and the corpus lives in it for years. Declared rather than inferred, exactly as A3 is.

tableAxis.description: How one axis of a table is keyed. Ticket 13's resolution of known unknown #2 found the axes HETEROGENEOUS: Table 26 keys on a thieving skill (an id), Table 28 on a Dexterity score (an integer), and Table 30 on a level BAND ('1-4', '5-8'). One kind would have fitted none of them. WIDENED by ticket 13 finding 138. Transcribing the v1 tier's remaining 90 tables found that MOST of them key on prose the pack has no record for — a light source, a coin, a tracking condition — which is exactly what finding 20 called a defect when a consumable table did it. The difference is declaration: `text` says the key is the book's own string and the Engine cannot index it, and such a table carries no `supplies` either. A3 applied to a table's axis, so that 'reference data a reader consults' and 'a table the Engine is waiting for' stop looking alike.

vocabulary.description: Required when kind is 'id': which enumeration the keys are drawn from, so the checker can refuse an unknown one.

tableValue.description: Ticket 13 finding 71: the Swashbuckler 'fights with the THAC0 of a FIGHTER of his experience level' — an effect that must READ a table belonging to another class. Names the field the table supplies, whose context it belongs to, and the index to read it at.

of.description: Whose table — a class entry, usually another class than the character's.

definition.description: Ticket 13 finding 101: a kit's named benefits and hindrances are things the kit BRINGS INTO BEING — 227 of them across 346 records, and 216 used exactly once, by the record that invented them. Given an id they are 216 references that can never resolve, because there is nothing to point at and nothing to transcribe: the definition IS the kit's own field. So the definition lives in the effect that grants it. The eleven used by more than one record are a different thing and keep their ids.

text.description: What the source says it does, in the source's words.

rollUnder.description: Ticket 13 finding 110. The demihuman detection abilities are all ONE shape — `1-5 on 1d6`, `1-7 on 1d10`, `1 on 1d6` — and the pack had nowhere to put it: `operand` was integer, computedOperand or tableValue, and `dice` was a value type NOTHING referenced (finding 42 said so and could not say why). A chance is not a number the corpus prints; writing 83% where the book writes `1-5 on 1d6` is inference, which A3 forbids. So the operand widens to hold the roll the book actually specifies, and `dice` finally has a consumer. 17 occurrences across the six player races; none in 1,121 kit effects, because kit bonuses are flat modifiers. **Correction 47: a rollUnder DENOTES A PROBABILITY, and the pack must be able to say so.** Writing 83% where the book writes `1-5 on 1d6` is inference and A3 forbids it, which is why the printed roll is what the record holds — but the refusal to infer was carried into the COMPARISON as well, and there it is wrong. The Player's Handbook gives the halfling's underground direction sense as `3- on 1d6` and the Complete Book of Gnomes and Halflings gives the Stout's as `50%`; **those are the same probability**, and the pack recorded a contradiction between two books that agree. The same pair agrees again on grade or slope, `3- on 1d4` against `75%`.\n\nSo: `rollAtMost n on 1dX` is the probability `n / X`, and a bare integer on a field that another layer writes as a rollUnder is a PERCENTAGE. The Engine converts before it compares, and the co-occurrence of the two forms on one field is itself the evidence that the field is a probability — which is why this needs no field-dimension vocabulary and does not wait on correction 23. **A3 governs what a record may CLAIM, not what a consumer may COMPUTE.**

rollAtMost.description: Success on this result or lower. `1-5 on 1d6` is 5.

provenanceMode.description: Ticket 12: §5.1 says the house-rule escape hatch IS the pack, so provenance cannot be unconditionally mandatory. Declared rather than inferred — A3 applied to provenance. **Correction 6 gave the declaration its consequence**: `extracted` means every record carries an `anchor` and the manifest names its `sources` by hash; `hand-authored` means no record carries an anchor and the pack names no sources. Enforced by the checker, since the condition spans the manifest and the records — two files, which a JSON Schema validates one at a time.

sources.description: Ticket 05: which source bytes this pack came from. Ticket 02 established that 'the DMG' is ambiguous with two byte-different variants in circulation. Correction 6: required when `provenanceMode` is `extracted`, and absent or empty when it is `hand-authored`.

declares.description: A3 (§5.1). Rule-set names are the Engine's closed enumeration — §3.4's single exception to open enumerations. Declarations scope to the subjects this pack introduces; the Engine unions them.

files.description: §7.1: declaration over discovery. A file present but unlisted is reported.

fields.description:
**Corrections 58 and 23.** Every field path this pack writes, declared. A path is an open string on purpose — §3.4 keeps enumerations open and the path is the escape hatch — and the cost of that was invisible until the Stout halfling wrote `detect.slopingPassage` where the dwarf, the gnome and the halfling all write `detect.gradeOrSlope`. **One ability, two paths, so the Player's Handbook's `3- on 1d4` and the Complete Book of Gnomes and Halflings' 75% never even collided.**

This is §7.1's manifest argument one level down: *declaration over discovery*. Scanning the effects for paths would let a near-synonym join the vocabulary in silence, exactly as scanning the directory would let a leftover file join the pack. A transcriber who must DECLARE `detect.slopingPassage` reads `detect.gradeOrSlope` on the line above it.

The checker reports a path written but not declared, and a path declared but never written — reported rather than failed, the same posture §7.1 takes for an undeclared file. `note` is optional: the declaring is the point, and 159 invented sentences would be worth less than the list.

NOT a closed enumeration and never becomes one. The Engine unions the declarations of every pack it loads, as it does for §5.1's rule-sets.

note.description: What it means, where the name does not say.

target.description: §4.1: a class entry, or the race.
§4.1: the race. §3.1: a Subrace is a Race with a parent reference.

items.description: Ticket 13 finding 107. §3.1 already says a Subrace IS a Race with a parent reference, and a Subrace is one of §4.1's three Attachable arms — so a Race carrying effects is not a new idea, it is the same idea the schema never granted the parent. A Race has NO target and NO prerequisite: it is not attached to a character, it is one of the things a character is.

classes.description: Ticket 13 findings 117 and 119. The most referenced thing in the pack and the last one with no kind: every Attachable names the class it attaches to, 171 of those references resolved to nothing, and the checker was not even counting them. Like `races` (finding 107) a class has NO target and NO prerequisite — it is not attached to a character, it is one of the things a character IS. Unlike a race it comes in two layers the corpus uses interchangeably: four GROUPS (warrior, wizard, priest, rogue) and nine classes inside them, and kits target both — `phb:priest` 22 times, `phb:cleric` 3. That is the same group/member split Table 44 gave weapons and Table 37 gave proficiencies, arriving a third time.

isGroup.description: True for the four groups. A group is targetable and owns the progression table.

group.description: The group this class belongs to. Absent on a group and on a multi-class.

combines.description: A multi-class arrangement, as §6.1's sum type: Fighter 5 / Mage 4 has no 'level 5', which is why `scalar.level` is always qualified by class.

abilityMinimums.description: Table 13. Absent where the table prints `Var` — the specialist wizard's minimums depend on the school, which is a fact about the school.

variantOf.description: Ticket 13 finding 137. The Complete Druid's eight BRANCHES — Arctic, Desert, Forest, Gray, Jungle, Mountain, Plains, Swamp — are a druid with a terrain, and the pack conditions on which one. §3.1 already says a Subrace is a Race with a parent reference; this is the same idea for a class, and the THIRD time the corpus has asked for it after Subrace and after the group/member split.

cost.description: As printed: '5 gp', '3sp/12'. Money is not an integer in this book.

damageType.description: P, S, B, or a combination.

groupKind.description:
**Correction 54: this field, and not `isGroup`, is now the whole statement that a record is a group — its presence says so and its value says which kind.** Before, sixteen table HEADINGS and twenty PRICED PROFICIENCY GROUPS both carried `isGroup: true` and both carried `members`, and the only thing telling them apart was that a priced group also carried `groupKind`. Inference by absence, and it caused a real error: asking whether a weapon's group-mates carried ammunition, the group 'Weapons Not Belonging To Any Group' put the blowgun beside the lasso and made the lasso look like a bow.

`heading` — Table 44 prints `Bow`, `Crossbow` and `Sword` over their variants, scoring nothing. A PRINTING convention: these rows appear under this name. Kits reference the heading far more often than a variant, so it is a record.
`tight` / `broad` — Ticket 13 finding 133. The Complete Fighter's turns grouping into a RULE: a Tight Group costs two proficiency slots and a Broad Group three. A PURCHASE, not a printing.
`none` — that book's name for the weapons belonging to no priced group, which must be bought one at a time. It has members and no `slotCost`, because it cannot be bought.

A heading and a priced group are not the same relation and the schema no longer spells them the same. `isGroup` is refused here outright (see `not`), so the ambiguous record is unrepresentable rather than merely wrong — §5. The `classes` kind keeps an `isGroup` of its own and it is a THIRD thing again: a class group owns a progression table and its membership points UPWARD, each class naming its `group`, where both weapon kinds point downward through `members`.

members.description: The weapons in the group, across books: a Fencing Blades group holds Table 44's dagger beside this book's rapier. Correction 49 gave the sixteen headings theirs, derived from the three spaces of indentation that are Table 44's only statement that a long bow is a Bow. Correction 54: what the membership MEANS is `groupKind`'s to say.

slotCost.description: Weapon proficiency slots to buy the whole group. Absent on a `none` group, which cannot be bought.

ammunition.description: Correction 53. **Eleven of Table 44's weapons carry no damage** — every bow, every crossbow, the sling, the staff sling, the blowgun — because in 2e the LAUNCHER has a speed factor and the AMMUNITION has the damage, and they are separate rows. Table 44 states the relation only by indenting the arrows under `Bow`; Table 45 states it properly, pairing 'Longbow, flight arrow' against 'Longbow, sheaf arrow' with different ranges. Without this field the pack cannot say what a long bow does, and `members` cannot carry it: ammunition is not a weapon you take proficiency in, and two of the launchers involved are not groups. Absent where the book never says — Table 45 gives the short bows one range line and names no arrow.

withAmmunition.description: Present only where the book prints a range PER AMMUNITION: Table 45 gives 'Longbow, flight arrow' 70/140/210 and 'Longbow, sheaf arrow' 50/100/170. Correction 53 found the damage living in the ammunition; the range lives in the PAIR.

range.description: **Correction 50.** Table 45 and the Complete Fighter's Missile Weapon Ranges, transcribed because of what they say about a weapon rather than for the ranges themselves: **sixteen kit bounds are stated over 'a melee weapon' or 'a missile weapon'**, and until now the pack had no way to tell them apart. It does now, and the distinction is three-way rather than two: a weapon with a range AND `ammunition` is a launcher; a weapon with a range and its own damage is a THROWN melee weapon; a weapon with no range is melee only. The Complete Fighter's Giant Killer makes the same distinction in prose — 'missile or hurled weapons'.\n\nDistances stay STRINGS, as cost and weight do: Table 45 prints the staff sling's short range as `--` and its medium as `30-60`.

items.description: Ticket 14 declared this kind with NO fields, before anything was transcribed. Its shape is Table 44's columns, set in session 51 the same way the nonweapon proficiency's four fields turned out to be Table 37's four columns — the book's own table IS the record shape.

group.description: Ticket 13 session 50: ticket 14 gave this kind a SINGLE group, written before anything was transcribed. PHB Table 37 puts 15 of its 65 proficiencies in TWO groups — a group is the list a class may buy from at normal cost, so belonging to two is what a crossover IS, not an anomaly. Widened to an array.

abilityCheck.description: A `scalar`, not a bare id. Absent for the two proficiencies Table 37 scores `NA` — Blind-fighting and Mountaineering have no ability check at all. Absent also where the book scores the ABILITY as special, as Intimidation does: 'ability special, special modifier'.

modifier.description: Ticket 13 finding 104: five Complete Thief's proficiencies score 'special modifiers' rather than a number — the modifier depends on circumstances the description sets out. Absent where a table scores NA; `special` where the book says so; an integer otherwise. The three states are different and the format now keeps them apart.

lookupTables.description: §3.1: named, typed table. XP progressions, THAC0, saving-throw matrices and thieving-skill adjustments are instances of it, owned by their class, group or race.

supplies.description: Ticket 13 finding 20 and its resolution: a table had an id derived from its source FILE, a name §7.3 says is never identity, and nothing saying what it was a table OF — so the Engine could not find the one it needed. It now names the FIELD PATH it fills, in the same vocabulary the effects use: a table supplying `thiefSkill` answers for `thiefSkill.openLocks`. Chosen over a second closed enumeration so that §3.4 keeps its single exception. Tables that supply no field — a list of permitted weapons, say — carry no `supplies` and the Engine does not consume them, which is A3's distinction applied to tables.

columnsAre.description: Present when the COLUMNS are a second axis rather than plain headings — Table 27 is (skill x race), Table 28 its transpose.

spheres.description: Ticket 13 finding 99: 64 reference occurrences pointed at priest SPHERES and no kind held them. A sphere is a named category a spell belongs to — the priest's side of what a school is for a wizard, and the two are the same shape used twice, exactly as §4.1's three Attachable arms are.

spellSchools.description: The wizard's side of the same shape. See `spheres`.

spells.description: Ticket 16 decision 1, taken: a spell is a REFERENCEABLE LABEL plus the six fields the book prints, kept as the book prints them. `Duration: 1 rd./level` stays a string — parsing it would grow the expression language across 470 records to answer a question the Engine has not been asked, since character generation casts nothing, and A3 makes an unparsed string honest rather than incomplete. What the spell DOES is prose and is not transcribed at all; that is stated here rather than left as an implied ambition.

schools.description: 43 of 303 wizard spells belong to MORE THAN ONE school, so this is a list. The spell pages abbreviate — `Evocation` for Invocation/Evocation, `Phantasm` for Illusion — and `Divination` resolves to the greater or the lesser school BY THE BOOK'S OWN RULE: 5th level or higher is greater. See ticket 13 finding 122.

schoolAsPrinted.description: The parenthetical exactly as the page prints it, kept because the mapping onto the nine schools is a reading and the reader must be able to check it.

spheres.description: 24 of 167 priest spells name more than one sphere.

sphereAsPrinted.description: `Elemental (Fire)` — the four elemental sub-spheres have no records, so the parenthetical survives here and the id is the sphere.

reversible.description: 65 spells print `Reversible` above the stat block. The reverse spell's own name is in the prose and is NOT transcribed.

armor.description: From Table 46's Armor Class Ratings. The table rates COMBINATIONS — 'leather or padded + shield' — so only the items the pack cites are recorded, at the rating the table gives them alone.

grantedAbilities.description: The eleven abilities used by MORE THAN ONE record. Everything used once is defined inline by the effect that grants it (`defines`, finding 101); these eleven are shared, and several are not kit inventions at all but CLASS abilities that kits reference — `phb:bard-spellcasting` is cited by three bard kits that take it away. WIDENED by ticket 13 finding 143. What the kind actually holds is broader than 'ability': it is ANYTHING THE RULES GRANT OR PERMIT THAT A RECORD MAY TAKE AWAY — a stronghold at 9th level, the bard's followers, the rank of Grand Druid, the permission to multi-class. None of these can be a `defines`, because `defines` is for what a record BRINGS INTO BEING and a kit that says 'no stronghold' is removing something the CLASS brought into being. The effect's own `kind` keeps naming the concept — `stronghold`, `follower`, `rank`, `classArrangement` — exactly as `phb:bard-spellcasting` has always been cited as `kind: ability`.

grantedBy.description: The class that grants it, where one does.

alignments.description: Ticket 13 finding 113. The last of finding 99's four homeless kinds — alignments, spheres, schools of magic and armour — and the one the corpus points at hardest: 49 of the pack's 166 unresolved reference occurrences. A closed list of nine, and NOT a flat one. The PHB opens the chapter by saying alignment 'is divided into two sets of attitudes: order and chaos, and good and evil', and that the nine are what COMBINING them produces — so the record carries the two axes, not just the label. An alignment has no effects: nothing in the PHB's chapter is a mechanic, which is why the kind has a shape and no `effects` array.

limitations.description: Ticket 16 decision 4, taken. Most of the pack's dangling ids were COMPLEMENTS — `weapons outside the Explorer's list`, `armor other than leather` — and a complement is not a record: it is the record's own sentence, so it becomes a `defines` (finding 101) and the id disappears. But eleven of them are reached by `except`, which alone among the six operations has NO `defines`, because its whole meaning is to lift a restriction that exists SOMEWHERE ELSE. Those somewhere-elses are real PHB rules — the thief's weapon list, the wizard's, the two-weapon penalty — and they get records here, owned by the class or the combat rule that imposes them. A limitation has no effects: it is a thing to be pointed AT. **Correction 48, from [Engine ticket 05]:** and, where the rule it names bounds a set, the SET ITSELF. Being a handle with no contents is what stopped 125 effects from being computable — a permit-list means ONLY these, and until the limitation held the members there was nothing for `forbid` to bound with or for `except` to lift. The field is optional on purpose: `phb:two-weapon-penalty` bounds nothing, and a restriction the pack's own vocabulary cannot express exactly is better left empty than populated with a set that permits more than the book does.

imposedBy.description: The class whose rule this is, where one owns it.

members.description: The things the rule PERMITS — not the things it forbids. Same shape as a `weaponProficiency` group's `members`, which twenty CFH records already carry, and deliberately the same field name: a bounded set is one concept whether a book prints it to price a proficiency slot or to restrict a class. An effect bounds a character by `forbid`-ing the limitation and lifts it by `except`-ing it, so `permitted = (∩ bounds) \ (∪ forbids)` — both operators commute, and §4.3's guarantee is inherited rather than re-argued. Absent means the limitation is a name only, which is what all seven were before this.

bounds.description:
**Correction 51.** The `kind` this limitation restricts, so that an effect naming it with a different one is a reportable disagreement rather than an invisible one — `phb:thief-weapon-restriction` was lifted as `weaponProficiency` three times and as `weapon` once, and nothing could see it.

**`weapon` and `weaponProficiency` are different restrictions and the books mark the difference with a VERB.** *May be proficient with*, *may choose*, *may only take*, *remaining slots must be spent on* — that is `weaponProficiency`. *Will never use*, *forbidden to*, *may use any weapon that is not* — that is `weapon`, and it is stronger, because PHB DD01528 lets anyone use any weapon at a to-hit penalty. A kit that says *use* is stating a vow the general rule does not impose.

Checked by the tool rather than the schema: a limitation and the effects that name it live in different files.

secondarySkills.description: Table 36's twenty-two, referenced by six kits and defined by nothing until now. The book names most of them as a PAIR — `Bowyer/Fletcher`, `Trapper/Furrier`, `Limner/Painter` — and the ids follow the book, not the half a transcriber happened to write (finding 96, fifth instance). `covers` is the parenthetical gloss the table prints, which is the only thing distinguishing a Forester from a Hunter.

proficiencyGroups.description: Ticket 13 finding 134. Every nonweapon proficiency has carried a `group` since session 50 and NOTHING DEFINED ONE — 83 reference occurrences, invisible because the checker walked a hand-listed set of paths and `group` was not on it. Table 37 prints five: the groups a class may buy from, which is a fact about the CLASS and not about the proficiency, exactly as §4.1's Attachable arms are about the character. `<book>:new` was an id the extractor invented for proficiencies whose group the book does not state; those now carry no group at all, which is A3.

openTo.description: The class groups that may buy from it, where Table 37 says so.

creatures.description: Ticket 13 finding 141. Correction 23 measured fourteen creature names living inside field-path STRINGS — `attackRoll.melee.vsOrc`, `opponent.attackRoll.titan` — because a `when` clause could describe the character and nothing else, so the other party had to hide in the path. These are NOT monster stat blocks: the Monstrous Manual is outside the v1 tier, and what a troll's hit dice are is not transcribed here. A creature record is a NAME THE RULES DISCRIMINATE ON, provenanced to the page that discriminates — the dwarf's entry, the gnome's — and it exists so that `{member: {field: 'opponent.creature'}, anyOfIds: [...]}` has something to point at.
